At the end of the 800-metre race in Cape Town, Zanele crossed the line second and bent over, hands on her knees, gasping. Her teammates swarmed her, shouting, patting her back. Marek pushed in closest, waving his phone. "Look, I filmed the whole thing!"
Zanele flapped a hand at him without looking up, a quick push-away wave.
Marek stepped back, his smile slipping. He lowered the phone and turned to go.
Zanele saw his face. She straightened, still panting. "Marek, wait. That wasn't 'go away.' That was 'I can't breathe yet.'"
He laughed, relieved. "Sorry. I crowded you."
"Just give me one minute of air. Then I want to see the video."
A minute later, they watched it together on the bench.

qa.a: The whole race.

qa.a: Marek felt hurt and rejected, thinking the wave meant she didn't want him there.

qa.a: She quickly added words to explain the wave meant she needed air, not that he should leave, and invited him back a minute later.

qa.a: Zanele felt overwhelmed and breathless, needing space to recover before she could enjoy the attention.

I'm sorry about the wedding. When the baraat reached the gate and everyone was pushing, you came up behind me and put your arm around my shoulder to pull me into the dancing. I shoved your arm off and waved you away, hard, without saying a word.

In Class 9, during a cricket match, Mridul kept calling me names every time I missed a ball. "Butterfingers! Useless!" The others started laughing.
I felt my fists clench. I wanted to shout back.
Instead, I put down the bat and said, "I'm going home. I'm not fighting." Then I walked away.
Mridul shouted, "Coward!" But I kept walking.
